newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu man has key mission in new Zaire government.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu man has key mission in new Zaire government.

text.p: Zaire's emergency rule prime minister has announced a new slimline government with a general close to embattled strongman Mobutu Sese Seko in the key post of interior minister.
But with rebels controlling half the sprawling Central African nation and Mobutu under growing pressure to stand down, sceptics suggested that the new administration had little room for manoeuvre.

Prime Minister Likulia Bolongo told a Friday news conference that fellow general Ilunga Shamanga, Mobutu's personal chief of staff, would take charge of the interior ministry "with the special mission of national reconciliation".

Likulia, appointed by Mobutu on Wednesday, named army chief of staff General Mahele Lieko Bokungu as his defence minister and renamed Kamanda wa Kamanda, a member of Kinshasa's team at talks with the rebels in South Africa, as his foreign minister.
"Our twin concern is to restore peace to the nation, conduct and pursue negotiations in South Africa but also to clean up public finances and demonstrate good governance," he said.
The new 28-member government's aim, he added, was to restore peace and security and ensure democracy and prosperity.
Many have their doubts. "Power is money and the army but we have neither. Our margin for manoeuvre has become tiny," one senior member of the new government said privately.

Likulia, Zaire's third prime minister in a week, said that Mahele had the task of national defence and restructuring Zaire's ragged and notoriously ill-disciplined army and turning it into a force that protected individual rights and freedoms.
Zaire's army, repeatedly routed by rebels who took up arms in October vowing to topple Mobutu, has a reputation for looting and terrorising civilians unfortunate enough to be in its path.

Mobutu, who has dominated Zaire since seizing power in 1965, declared a nationwide state of emergency on Tuesday and then shunted aside his arch-foe, veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, who had been prime minister for less than a week.
Mobutu, 66, had prostate cancer surgery in Europe in August. He is now back in Kinshasa.
Laurent Kabila, whose rebels now control Zaire's economic heartland, has given Mobutu until this weekend to show a willingness to quit -- or face fresh advances on all fronts.
The rebels captured Zaire's second city of Lubumbashi, capital of mineral-rich Shaba province, on Wednesday and Thursday. It is their biggest prize to date.
Ordinary Zaireans hail Kabila as a liberator. Mobutu's traditional friends are distancing themselves from him.

The United States and former colonial power Belgium have urged him to stand down. France, which has long backed Mobutu, publicly urged him to meet Kabila face-to-face in the interests of peace -- something he has rejected out-of-hand.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan has urged the two sides to resume talks in South Africa, calling for a peaceful settlement to lead Zaire to democracy.
South Africa's deputy president, Thabo Mbeki, host of first round talks last week, said he expected negotiations would resume early next week -- with Mobutu's future on the agenda.
On the humanitarian front, the U.N. said it flew 240 displaced Zaireans to the eastern border town of Goma in a test run for the repatriation of up to 100,000 Rwandan refugees.
